column4: ch-018 chunk 1 (Gibb: Zayla, Mogadishu, Mombasa, Kulwa)
column5: Gibb's translation: Ibn Battuta left Mecca after the pilgrimage at the close of 1330, sailed to Zayla, Maqdashaw (Mogadishu: slaughters hundreds of camels a day, host system, sultan Abu Bakr, Berberah origin), Mombasa (an island, wooden mosques, bananas and fish), then Kulwa, which he calls a very fine town, mostly Zanj, with sultan Abu'l-Muzaffar Hasan (generous) succeeded by his brother Dawud (miserly); a merchant told him Sufala is a fortnight south and gold dust comes there from Yufi. Supports the course's about 1330 to 1331 Kilwa range (his own sailing starts after the pilgrimage ending 1330). Note the translation says his hosts' buildings at Kulwa are of wood, which the lesson's coral-stone Husuni Kubwa picture should not contradict silently: Husuni Kubwa is the palace-warehouse the archaeology shows; his remark is one visitor's report. OCR quality poor; quote nothing.

column4: ch-036 chunk 1 (editor's notes to the Sahara chapter, note 21 and 31)
column5: Gibb's 1929 notes give the old textbook chronology: Ghana destroyed by the Almoravids in 1076, Sunjata d. 1255, Musa reigning 1307-32, Maghan 1332-6, Sulayman 1336-59, Songhay under Sonni Ali 1464-92 and Askia Muhammad 1493-1529, Moroccan capture of Gao and Timbuktu in 1591, Mossi burned Timbuktu in 1333, and as-Sahili (poet and architect, died 1346 at Timbuktu) built the mosques at Gao and Timbuktu. These are an older editor's summary, not evidence. The Almoravid destruction of Ghana is the claim Module 3 tags [CONTESTED]; the as-Sahili note supports the course's architect line but is a 20th-century editor's reading. The notes also identify Wangara as Soninke and Malinke, Takedda as Berber, and Gao's salt and trans-Saharan routes.

column4: ch-029 chunk 1 (Sijilmasa to Taghaza to Walata)
column5: Gibb's translation: left Sijilmasa Muharram 753 (18/02/1352) with a caravan, reached Taghaza in 25 days (houses and mosque of salt blocks, slave diggers of the Massufa, a camel carries two slabs, salt worth 8-10 mithqals at Walata and 20-40 at Mali, salt used as currency), then a desert crossing with a hired guide (takshif) to Walata, two months from Sijilmasa. Eyewitness for the Module 3 route and goods lesson: salt south, and the price jump with distance. Quote nothing (OCR poor).

column4: ch-029 chunk 1 (Walata and Mali capital, Mansa Sulayman)
column5: Ibn Battuta at Walata: people take heirs through the mother's brother, women unveiled and free to have male companions, which shocked him; 24 days to Mali; at Mali he met the qadi (a Black pilgrim), the interpreter Dugha, fell ill two months; Mansa Sulayman was mean (his first gift was bread, beef and curds), later 33 and a third mithqals alms and 100 mithqals on leaving; audiences on a platform with silk umbrella topped by a golden bird, 300 armed slaves, subjects throwing dust on their heads. Confirms the course's Module 4 lesson 2 and lecturer lesson (matrilineal succession, court ceremony, praise and criticism). He mistakes the Niger for the Nile (editor's note).

column4: ch-029 chunk 2 (Mali festivals, justice, dates, Timbuktu, Gao)
column5: Gibb: at Mali on festival days Dugha leads praise-singing with poets in bird costumes; Ibn Battuta praises the people's hatred of injustice, security for travellers and safe-keeping of dead whites' property, Friday devotion, Koran learning (children chained until memorised), and criticises women's nakedness, dust on heads and eating carrion. Dates: arrived Mali 14 Jumada I 753 (28/06/1352), left 22 Muharram 754 (27/02/1353): the course's 1352-53 is right. He says Mansa Musa was generous and gave as-Sahili 4,000 mithqals in one day, and reports a cannibal-embassy tale and a hippopotamus hunt (hearsay). Timbuktu: a Massufa town four miles from the river with as-Sahili's grave; Gao: a large city using cowries as money. He calls the Niger the Nile. Confirms Module 4 lesson 2 and the lecturer lesson; the cannibal story is hearsay [THIN EVIDENCE].

column4: ch-029 chunk 2 (Takedda copper, slaves, route to Tawat)
column5: Gibb: at Tagadda (Takedda) copper bars were money (400 thick bars to a mithqal of gold) and were exported to Kubar, Zaghay and Barnu; the people lived by trade and slaves; Ibn Battuta bought an educated slave girl for 25 mithqals; he left Tagadda on 11 Sha'ban 754 (11/09/1353) in a caravan with six hundred women slaves, crossing Ahaggar. An eyewitness for Module 3 goods and slave flows (copper and slaves as well as salt and gold). Prices are his, in mithqals.
